The First Discourse on Arhatship:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five? [The text continues with the enumeration of the five faculties.]”
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When, monks,
a noble disciple has understood as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, and is liberated through non-clinging,

he is called, monks, a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through final knowledge.”

The First Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.
Which five?”
The faculty of faith ... [and so on] ... the faculty of wisdom.

For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five faculties, those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, are not ascetics among ascetics, nor are they brahmins among brahmins.

They are esteemed by brahmins, yet these venerable ones do not themselves, through direct knowledge, realize and dwell in the attainment of the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood in this very life.

But those, monks, who— whether ascetics or brahmins— understand as they really are the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five faculties, [they are the true ascetics and brahmins].
“Those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, are indeed reckoned as ascetics among ascetics and as brahmins among brahmins;
and those venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the goal of the ascetic life and the goal of the brahmin life, enter and dwell therein.”

The Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins:
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand the faculty of faith, do not understand the origin of the faculty of faith,
do not understand the cessation of the faculty of faith, and do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith;”
They do not understand the faculty of energy … [and so on] … they do not understand the faculty of mindfulness … [and so on] … they do not understand the faculty of concentration … [and so on] …

They do not understand the faculty of wisdom; they do not understand the arising of the faculty of wisdom; they do not understand the cessation of the faculty of wisdom; they do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of wisdom.
Monks, those recluses or brahmins are not, among recluses, reckoned as recluses, nor among brahmins, reckoned as brahmins.
Furthermore, these venerable ones do not, in this very life, [attain] the goal of the recluse or the goal of the brahmin.
They dwell having realized for themselves through direct knowledge and having attained these states.
And as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who understand the faculty of faith, who understand the origin of the faculty of faith,
who understand the cessation of the faculty of faith, and who understand the way leading to the cessation of the faculty of faith;

They understand the faculty of energy, they understand the origin of the faculty of energy, they understand the cessation of the faculty of energy, and they understand the practice leading to the cessation of the faculty of energy;
they understand the faculty of mindfulness ... [and so on] ...
they understand the faculty of concentration ... [and so on].

They understand the faculty of wisdom; they understand the origin of the faculty of wisdom; they understand the cessation of the faculty of wisdom; they understand the way leading to the cessation of the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, whether recluses or brahmins, are reckoned among the recluses as true recluses and among the brahmins as true brahmins;
and these venerable ones, in this very life, have realized the goal of the recluse and the goal of the brahmin.
“Having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, I dwell having attained it.

1. Suddhikavagga Daṭṭhabbasutta “Bhikkhus,
there are these five faculties.”
Which five?
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
And where, monks, is the faculty of faith to be seen?
Among the four factors of stream-entry—
herein the faculty of faith is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the faculty of energy to be seen?
In the four right endeavors—
the faculty of energy is to be seen here.
And where, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness to be seen?
Among the four foundations of mindfulness,
it is here that the faculty of mindfulness is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the faculty of concentration to be seen?
In the four jhānas—
herein the faculty of concentration is to be seen.
And where, monks, is the faculty of wisdom to be seen?
“Among the four noble truths—
in this context, the faculty of wisdom is to be seen.
These, monks, are the five faculties.”
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.9 (SN 48.9, PTS SN v 196) 1.
The Chapter on the Simple (Suddhika-vagga)
The First Analysis Discourse:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.
Which five?”
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of faith?
Here, bhikkhus, the noble disciple is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: [text continues]

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One’—this, monks, is called the faculty of faith.
And what, monks, is the faculty of energy?

"Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
This, monks, is called the faculty of energy.
And what, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness?"
"Here, monks, a noble disciple is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
This, monks, is called the faculty of mindfulness.
And what, monks, is the faculty of concentration?"
"Here, monks, a noble disciple, having made relinquishment the object, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind— this, monks,
is called the faculty of concentration.
And what, monks, is the faculty of wisdom?"

“Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering—this, monks, is called the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.10 (SN 48.10, PTS SN v 197) 1.
The Chapter on the Pure (Suddhika-vagga)
The Second Analysis Discourse:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.
Which five?”
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
And what, bhikkhus, is the faculty of faith?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One’—this, monks, is called the faculty of faith.
And what, monks, is the faculty of energy?

"Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen."
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen;

he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
This, monks, is called the faculty of energy.
And what, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects even what was done long ago and spoken long ago.
Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in relation to feelings …pe… in relation to the mind …pe…
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
this, monks, is called the faculty of mindfulness.
And what, monks, is the faculty of concentration?
In this case, monks, a noble disciple, having made relinquishment his object, attains concentration; he attains one-pointedness of mind.

Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and singleness of mind, without applied or sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called the faculty of concentration.
And what, monks, is the faculty of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise;
he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus one understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; one understands as it really is:
“This is the cessation of suffering”; one understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
This, monks, is called the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties. Thus ends the tenth [sutta].
The first chapter: The Pure Section.
Its summary verse:
The pure [jhānas], and two streams.
Two others are Arahants;
the recluses and brahmins are to be seen,

Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.11 Mudutaravagga Paṭilābhasutta “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of obtaining what has not yet been obtained, of achieving what has not yet been achieved, of realizing what has not yet been realized. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, is virtuous, is learned, is energetic, and possesses wisdom. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of obtaining what has not yet been obtained, of achieving what has not yet been achieved, of realizing what has not yet been realized.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith … [as above] … the faculty of wisdom … [as above] …”
And what, monks, is the faculty of faith?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus:

“The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.”
This, monks, is called the faculty of faith.
And what, monks, is the faculty of energy?
It is that energy, monks, which one acquires by undertaking the four right strivings.
This, monks, is called the faculty of energy.
And what, monks, is the faculty of mindfulness?
It is that mindfulness, monks, which one acquires by taking up the four foundations of mindfulness.
This, monks, is called the faculty of mindfulness.
And what, monks, is the faculty of concentration?
Here, monks, a noble disciple, having made relinquishment the object, attains concentration; he attains one-pointedness of mind.
This, monks, is called the faculty of concentration.
And what, monks, is the faculty of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise;
he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
"This, monks, is called the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties. Thus [ends] the first.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.12 2. Mudutaravagga First Discourse on the Brief “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to attend upon him, to wait upon him, and to serve him. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He is very learned, one who has mastered the Dhamma—those discourses that are in the beginning excellent, in the middle excellent, and in the end excellent, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—and he retains them in mind, recites them verbally, contemplates them with the mind, and penetrates them well through view. He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. He possesses the wisdom that arises from seclusion, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to attend upon him, to wait upon him, and to serve him.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith … [as above] … the faculty of wisdom.”
These, monks, are the five faculties.
By the fulfillment and perfection of these five faculties, one is an arahant;
by those that are weaker than those, one is a non-returner; by those that are weaker than those, one is a once-returner; by those that are weaker than those, one is a stream-enterer.
“...from that, one becomes a follower by Dhamma through weaker qualities; from that, one becomes a follower by faith through even weaker qualities.
This is the second.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.”

The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom—
these, monks, are the five faculties.
“Monks, it is through the fulfillment and perfection of these five faculties that one becomes an arahant;
with them being weaker than that, one becomes a non-returner; with them being weaker than that, one becomes a once-returner; with them being weaker than that, one becomes a stream-enterer;
with them being weaker than that, one becomes a follower by Dhamma; and with them being weaker than that, one becomes a follower by faith.”
“Thus, monks, diversity in the faculties leads to diversity in the fruits; diversity in the fruits leads to diversity in persons.
This was the third [discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 48.14 (SN 48.14, PTS SN v 201)
2. Mudutaravagga.
Third Short Discourse:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.”
Which five?
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom—
these, monks, are the five faculties.
“Monks, through the completion and fulfillment of these five faculties one becomes an arahant;
with them being weaker than that, one becomes a non-returner; with them being weaker than that, one becomes a once-returner; with them being weaker than that, one becomes a stream-enterer;

“Thus, monks, one who acts completely fulfills what is complete; one who acts partially fulfills what is partial.
‘The five faculties, monks, are indeed not barren,’ I say. This is the fourth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 48.15 (SN 48.15, PTS SN v 201) 2. Mudutaravagga First Discourse on Expansion “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is narrow-minded and narrow in his talk; the person who is narrow-minded but broad in his talk; the person who is broad-minded but narrow in his talk; and the person who is broad-minded and broad in his talk. And how, monks, is a person narrow-minded and narrow in his talk? Here, monks, a certain person is of little learning, one who has not mastered the Dhamma—those discourses that are deep, profound, transcendent, connected with the Void, and which, when spoken, are not easily understood by those who are ordinary. This, monks, is called a person who is narrow-minded and narrow in his talk. And how, monks, is a person narrow-minded but broad in his talk? Here, monks, a certain person is of little learning, one who has not mastered the Dhamma—those discourses that are deep, profound, transcendent, connected with the Void, and which, when spoken, are not easily understood by those who are ordinary. Yet he speaks much about the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a person who is narrow-minded but broad in his talk. And how, monks, is a person broad-minded but narrow in his talk? Here, monks, a certain person is learned, one who has mastered the Dhamma—those discourses that are deep, profound, transcendent, connected with the Void, and which, when spoken, are not easily understood by those who are ordinary. Yet he does not speak much about the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a person who is broad-minded but narrow in his talk. And how, monks, is a person broad-minded and broad in his talk? Here, monks, a certain person is learned, one who has mastered the Dhamma—those discourses that are deep, profound, transcendent, connected with the Void, and which, when spoken, are not easily understood by those who are ordinary. And he speaks much about the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a person who is broad-minded and broad in his talk. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith … [as above] … the faculty of wisdom.”
These, monks, are the five faculties.
Through the fulfillment and perfection of these five faculties, one becomes an arahant;
with faculties weaker than those, one becomes one who attains nibbāna in the interval; with faculties weaker than those, one becomes one who attains nibbāna upon landing.
“If they are weaker still, one attains final nibbāna without exertion; if they are weaker still, one attains final nibbāna with exertion;
if they are weaker still, one becomes a non-returner bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; if they are weaker still, one becomes a once-returner; if they are weaker still, one becomes a stream-enterer;
if they are weaker still, one becomes a follower by Dhamma; and if they are weaker still, one becomes a follower by faith.”
Fifth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.16 (SN 48.16, PTS SN v 201) 2.
Mudutaravagga (The Chapter on the Soft-voiced One)
The Second Discourse on Expansion:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom—these, monks, are the five faculties.
Through the fulfillment and completion of these five faculties, one becomes an arahant; beyond that, there is nothing further.
With still weaker faculties, one becomes an attainer of nibbāna in the interval; with still weaker faculties, one becomes an attainer of nibbāna upon landing;
with still weaker faculties, one becomes an attainer of nibbāna without exertion; with still weaker faculties, one becomes an attainer of nibbāna with exertion;
with still weaker faculties, one becomes a non-returner bound upstream for the Akaniṭṭha realm; with still weaker faculties, one becomes a once-returner; and with still weaker faculties...
When these are weaker still, one is a stream-enterer; when they are weaker still than that, one is a follower by Dhamma; when they are weaker still than that, one is a follower by faith.
Thus, monks, diversity in the faculties leads to diversity in the fruits; diversity in the fruits leads to diversity in persons. This was the sixth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 48.17 (SN 48.17, PTS SN v 202) 2. Mudutaravagga Tatiyavitthārasutta (The Third Discourse on Expansion) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is expanding; the person who is contracting; the person who is both expanding and contracting; and the person who is neither expanding nor contracting. And how, monks, is one a person who is expanding? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind that is expansive, vast, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. This is called a person who is expanding. And how, monks, is one a person who is contracting? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind that is cramped, inferior, limited, and accompanied by enmity and ill will. This is called a person who is contracting. And how, monks, is one a person who is both expanding and contracting? Here, monks, a certain person dwells sometimes with a mind that is expansive, vast, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will; and sometimes he dwells with a mind that is cramped, inferior, limited, and accompanied by enmity and ill will. This is called a person who is both expanding and contracting. And how, monks, is one a person who is neither expanding nor contracting? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the fetter of form, severed the desire for existence, and, through the complete destruction of ignorance, attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is called a person who is neither expanding nor contracting. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith … [as above] … the faculty of wisdom.”
These, monks, are the five faculties.
Through the fulfillment and perfection of these five faculties, one becomes an arahant;
with faculties weaker than those, one becomes one who attains nibbāna in the interval; with faculties weaker than those, one becomes one who attains nibbāna upon landing.
If these are weaker, one is an attainer of nibbāna without exertion; if weaker than that, one is an attainer of nibbāna with exertion;
if weaker than that, one is a non-returner bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm; if weaker than that, one is a once-returner; if weaker than that, one is a stream-enterer;
if weaker than that, one is a follower by Dhamma; and if weaker than that, one is a follower by faith.
"Thus, monks, one who acts fully achieves the full; one who acts partially achieves the partial.
'The five faculties, monks, are indeed not barren,' I say. This was the seventh [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 48.18 (SN 48.18, PTS SN v 202) 2. Mudutaravagga Paṭipannasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who is practicing the way, the one who has attained the fruit, the one who has fallen away from the fruit, and the one who is neither practicing nor attained. These, bhikkhus, are the four persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.”
These, monks, are the five faculties.
By the completion and fulfillment of these five faculties, one is an arahant;
with those that are weaker than that, one is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship; with those that are weaker than that, one is a non-returner.
Then, with weaker [faculties], one is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; then, with weaker [faculties], one is a once-returner;
then, with weaker [faculties], one is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning;
then, with weaker [faculties], one is a stream-enterer; then, with weaker [faculties], one is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
“Monks, whoever lacks these five faculties entirely, in every way and in all respects, of him I say: ‘He stands outside, on the side of the worldlings.
This was the eighth [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 48.19.
2. The Chapter on the Soft-Toned (Mudutaravagga):

The Discourse on Being Endowed (Sampannasutta) Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one endowed with the faculties, one endowed with the faculties.
In what way, venerable sir, is one endowed with the faculties?
“In this case, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment; he develops the faculty of energy...”
He develops the faculty of mindfulness, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment;
he develops the faculty of concentration, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment; he develops the faculty of wisdom, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment.
To this extent, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu is endowed with the faculties.”
The Ninth.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. [The Buddha spoke thus. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir; it is marvelous, venerable sir! How the Blessed One has proclaimed the destruction of the taints through these very five faculties! “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! It is wonderful, Ānanda, that the Tathāgata has proclaimed the destruction of the taints through these very five faculties. For, Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these five faculties, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. When a noble disciple possesses these five faculties, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life. [The Blessed One spoke thus. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does a noble disciple possess the faculty of faith such that he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure The First Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in regard to this final knowledge itself? “Bhikkhu, the gratification in the case of this final knowledge is the peace and happiness that arise from it; the danger is its conditioned nature; the escape is the liberation of the mind through non-clinging. When this was said, yet another bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape in regard to this liberation of the mind through non-clinging? “Bhikkhu, the gratification in the case of this liberation of the mind through non-clinging is the peace and happiness that arise from it; the danger is its being a conditioned phenomenon; the escape is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very liberation of the mind. The First Analysis Discourse:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.
Which five?”
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
And what, monks, is the faculty of pleasure?
Whatever, monks, is bodily pleasure, bodily well-being, pleasure born of body-contact, a pleasant feeling experienced by the body—this is called the faculty of pleasure.
This, monks, is called the faculty of pleasure.
And what, monks, is the faculty of pain?
Whatever is bodily pain, bodily discomfort, the painful and unpleasant feeling born of body-contact—this, monks, is called the faculty of pain.
This, monks, is called the faculty of suffering.
And what, monks, is the faculty of mental pleasure?
That which is mental happiness, mental well-being, the pleasant and agreeable feeling born of mind-contact—this, monks, is called the faculty of mental pleasure.
This, monks, is called the faculty of mental pleasure.
And what, monks, is the faculty of mental pain?
Whatever is mental suffering, mental unpleasantness, the painful and unpleasant feeling born of mind-contact—this, monks, is called the faculty of mental pain.
This, monks, is called the faculty of mental distress.
And what, monks, is the faculty of equanimity?
That which, monks, is felt as neither pleasant nor unpleasant, whether bodily or mental—this is the faculty of equanimity.
This, monks, is called the faculty of equanimity.
These, monks, are the five faculties. Thus ends the sixth [discourse].

This is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these five faculties and understands these four noble truths as they really are, he is called a stream-enterer... with enlightenment as his destination. “This, bhikkhus, is the analysis of these five faculties by way of their distinction, by way of their penetration, by way of their final arrival, and by way of their final liberation. 4. The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure:
The Third Exposition Sutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.”
Which five?
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
And what, monks, is the faculty of pleasure?
“Monks, whatever is bodily pleasure, bodily well-being, the pleasant and agreeable feeling born of body-contact—
this, monks, is called the faculty of pleasure.
And what, monks, is the faculty of pain?”
Whatever, monks, is bodily pain, bodily unpleasantness, painful and unpleasant feeling born of body-contact—
this, monks, is called the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*).
And what, monks, is the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*)?
"Monks, that which is mental pleasure, mental well-being, the pleasant and well-felt experience born of mind-contact—
this, monks, is called the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).
And what, monks, is the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*)?"
"Whatever, monks, is mental suffering, mental displeasure, the painful and unpleasant feeling born of mind-contact—
this, monks, is called the faculty of grief.
And what, monks, is the faculty of equanimity?"
“Monks, whatever feeling is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, whether bodily or mental— this, monks,
is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
In this regard, monks, both the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy are to be regarded as pleasant feeling.”
“In this regard, monks, that which is the faculty of pain and that which is the faculty of mental grief—these should be regarded as painful feeling.
In this regard, monks, that which is the faculty of equanimity—this should be regarded as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure (Sukhindriyavagga)
The Simile of the Log Sutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. Which five?
The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
Dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, bhikkhus, the faculty of pleasure arises.
Being pleased, one understands: "I am pleased."

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, he understands: ‘That faculty of pleasure which arose dependent on the contact to be experienced as pleasant ceases; it subsides.
Monks, the faculty of pain arises dependent on contact to be experienced as painful.
Being pained, he understands: ‘I am pained.’
“With the cessation of that very same contact to be experienced as painful, he understands: ‘That faculty of pain which arose in dependence on the contact to be experienced as painful—that ceases;
it subsides. Monks, the faculty of joy arises in dependence on contact to be experienced as joyful.
Being joyful, he understands: ‘I am joyful.’”
With the cessation of that very same contact to be experienced as joy, he understands: ‘That faculty of joy which arose dependent on the contact to be experienced as joy—that ceases; it subsides.
Monks, dependent on contact to be experienced as displeasure, the faculty of displeasure arises.
Being displeased, he understands: ‘I am displeased.’

“With the cessation of that very same contact to be experienced as displeasure, he understands: ‘That faculty of displeasure which arose in dependence on the contact to be experienced as displeasure—that ceases; it subsides.
Monks, the faculty of equanimity arises in dependence on contact to be experienced as equanimity.
Being equanimous, he understands: ‘I am equanimous.’”

“Monks, with the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as equanimity, one understands: ‘That faculty of equanimity which arose dependent on the contact to be experienced as equanimity—that ceases, that subsides.

Monks, just as when two pieces of wood rub together and meet, heat is produced and fire is generated, but with the separation and removal of those very pieces of wood, that corresponding heat ceases and subsides;”
In the same way, monks, in dependence on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, the faculty of pleasure arises.
Being happy, he understands: "I am happy.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, he understands: "That feeling which was to be experienced as pleasant, arising in dependence on that contact—the faculty of pleasure—ceases; it subsides."

“Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful … [and so on] … dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, monks … dependent on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, monks … dependent on a contact to be experienced as mental joy,
monks … dependent on a contact to be experienced as mental grief, monks …” [and so on].
“Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as equanimity, the faculty of equanimity arises.
Being equanimous, he understands: ‘I am equanimous.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as equanimity, he understands: ‘That feeling pertaining to it—the faculty of equanimity which arose dependent on the contact to be experienced as equanimity—ceases; it subsides.’”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.40 (SN 48.40, PTS SN v 213) 4.
The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure (Sukhindriyavagga)
The Discourse on the Irregular Order:
“Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties.
Which five?”
The faculty of pain, the faculty of mental grief, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of mental joy, and the faculty of equanimity.
Here, monks, while a monk dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, the faculty of pain arises.
He understands thus:
‘This arisen faculty of pain has a cause, a source, a condition, and a basis;
it is impossible that a faculty of pain without a cause, without a source, without a condition, and without a basis should arise.

He understands the faculty of pain, he understands the origin of the faculty of pain, he understands the cessation of the faculty of pain, and he understands where the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder?

Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion;
it is here that the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder.
“Monks, this is called a monk who has understood the cessation of the faculty of suffering and directs his mind toward that end.
Furthermore, monks, while a monk dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, the faculty of mental distress arises within him.
He understands thus:”
‘This faculty of mental grief has arisen in me, and it is with a sign, with a source, with volitional formations, and with a condition.
It is impossible that a faculty of mental grief without a sign, without a source, without volitional formations, and without a condition could arise.

He understands the faculty of mental grief; he understands the origin of the faculty of mental grief; he understands the cessation of the faculty of mental grief; and he understands where the arisen faculty of mental grief ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of mental grief cease without remainder?

Here, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness;
it is here that the arisen faculty of mental grief ceases without remainder.
“Monks, this is called a bhikkhu who has understood the cessation of the faculty of mental distress and directs his mind toward that end.
Furthermore, monks, while a bhikkhu dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, the faculty of pleasure arises within him.
He understands thus:”
‘This pleasure faculty has arisen in me, and it is with a sign, with a source, with volitional formations, and with a condition.
It is impossible that a pleasure faculty without a sign, without a source, without volitional formations, and without a condition could arise’—this is not possible.

He understands the pleasure faculty; he understands the origin of the pleasure faculty; he understands the cessation of the pleasure faculty; and he understands where the arisen pleasure faculty ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of pleasure cease without remainder?
Here, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body;
of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. This is where the arisen faculty of pleasure ceases without remainder.
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna;
herein, the arisen faculty of pleasure ceases without remainder.
This, monks, is called: “A monk has understood the cessation of the faculty of pleasure; he directs his mind toward that end.”
But here, monks, while a monk dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, the faculty of mental joy arises in him.
He understands thus:
"This faculty of mental joy has arisen in me; and it is accompanied by a sign, accompanied by a cause, accompanied by volitional formations, and accompanied by conditions."
‘That signless, causeless, unconditioned, and groundless faculty of joy will arise’—this is impossible.

He understands the faculty of joy; he understands the origin of the faculty of joy; he understands the cessation of the faculty of joy; and he understands where the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of joy cease without remainder?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity;
herein, the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder.
“Monks, this is called a monk who has understood the cessation of the faculty of mental joy and directs his mind toward that end.
Furthermore, monks, as a monk dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, the faculty of equanimity arises within him.
He understands thus:”
‘This equanimity faculty has arisen in me, and it is with a sign, with a source, with volitional formations, and with a condition.
It is impossible that an equanimity faculty without a sign, without a source, without volitional formations, and without a condition will arise’—this is not possible.

He understands the equanimity faculty; he understands the arising of the equanimity faculty; he understands the cessation of the equanimity faculty; and he understands where the arisen equanimity faculty ceases without remainder.
Where does the arisen faculty of equanimity cease without remainder?
Here, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
it is here that the arisen faculty of equanimity ceases without remainder.
“Monks, this is called a monk who has understood the cessation of the equanimity faculty and directs his mind toward that end.
Tenth. The Fourth Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure.
Its summary verse:
The pure one, the stream-enterer, and the arahant;
the two types of ascetics and brahmins.

the "wood" and the "out-of-order.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 48.41 (SN 48.41, PTS SN v 216).
5. The Chapter on Aging:
The Discourse on the Nature of Aging Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, the Blessed One was sitting in the western sun, warming his back.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, while stroking the Blessed One’s limbs with his hand, he said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!

Venerable sir, the Blessed One’s complexion is no longer so pure and bright; all his limbs are flaccid and wrinkled, his body is bent forward, and a change in the faculties is apparent—the faculty of the eye, the faculty of the ear, the faculty of the nose, the faculty of the tongue, and the faculty of the body.”
“It is indeed so, Ānanda:
youth is subject to aging, health is subject to illness, and life is subject to death.
The complexion of the skin is not yet completely pure and bright; all the limbs become flaccid and covered with wrinkles; the body bends forward; and a change in the faculties is evident.”
“Of the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Shame on that wretched old age;
may there be an end to this old age that makes one disfigured!
For how long will this enchanting form [last]?”
Crushed by old age—
even one who lives for a hundred years is destined for death.
It avoids nothing at all;
it crushes everything. Thus ends the first [verse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.42 (SN 48.42, PTS SN v 217) 5. Jarāvagga Uṇṇābhabrāhmaṇasutta – The Discourse to the Brahmin Uṇṇābha At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging: those I do not consider to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and those venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood. But whatever ascetics or brahmins understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to these five aggregates subject to clinging: those I consider to be ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins, and those venerable ones, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. Furthermore, brahmin, someone dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, burning with restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. Furthermore, brahmin, someone dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, burning with doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. As he dwells thus, the path leading to the cessation of ill will arises in him. He understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Furthermore, brahmin, someone dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells thus, the path leading to the cessation of dullness and drowsiness arises in him. He understands as it really is the escape from the arisen dullness and drowsiness. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Furthermore, brahmin, someone dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells thus, the path leading to the cessation of restlessness and remorse arises in him. He understands as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Furthermore, brahmin, someone dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells thus, the path leading to the cessation of doubt arises in him. He understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. It is, brahmin, because they have developed and cultivated these four foundations of mindfulness that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. When this was said, the brahmin Uṇṇābha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the brahmin Uṇṇābha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Uṇṇābha said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, there are these five faculties that have different domains and different ranges, and they do not experience each other’s domain and range.
Which five?
The eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty.”

“Master Gotama, what is the refuge for these five faculties, which have different domains and different ranges, and which do not experience each other’s range and domain? And who is it that experiences their range and domain?
“Brahmin, these five faculties have different domains and different ranges; they do not experience each other’s range and domain.”
“What are the five?
The eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty.

“But what, Master Gotama, is the resort of the mind?

"Or by anything else in the world.

Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in the Añjana Grove, the Deer Park.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Is there, monks, a method by which, relying on that method, those which are the five faculties are the five powers, and those which are the five powers are the five faculties?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it. …pe…
“There is, bhikkhus, a method by means of which those that are the five faculties are the five powers, and those that are the five powers are the five faculties.
And what, bhikkhus, is that method by means of which those that are the five faculties are the five powers, and those that are the five powers are the five faculties?
That which is the faculty of faith is the power of faith; that which is the power of faith is the faculty of faith.
That which is the faculty of energy is the power of energy, and that which is the power of energy is the faculty of energy;
that which is the faculty of mindfulness is the power of mindfulness, and that which is the power of mindfulness is the faculty of mindfulness;
that which is the faculty of concentration is the power of concentration, and that which is the power of concentration is the faculty of concentration.
That which is the faculty of wisdom is the power of wisdom; that which is the power of wisdom is the faculty of wisdom.

Just as, monks, there is a river flowing eastward, inclining eastward, sloping eastward, with an island in its midst—there is, monks, a way of accounting by which, according to that method, that river is reckoned as having only a single stream.
"But there is, monks, a way of accounting by which that river comes to be reckoned as having two streams.
And what, monks, is the way of accounting by which that river comes to be reckoned as having but one stream?
It is, monks, the water on the eastern side of that island and the water on the western side."
This, monks, is the method by which that river comes to be reckoned as having only a single stream.
And what, monks, is the method by which that river comes to be reckoned as having two streams?
It is the water on the northern side of that island, monks, and the water on the southern side.
This, monks, is the method by which that river comes to be reckoned as having two streams.
In the same way, monks, that which is the faculty of faith is the power of faith, and that which is the power of faith is the faculty of faith;
that which is the faculty of energy is the power of energy, and that which is the power of energy is the faculty of energy.
That which is the faculty of mindfulness is the power of mindfulness; that which is the power of mindfulness is the faculty of mindfulness.
That which is the faculty of concentration is the power of concentration; that which is the power of concentration is the faculty of concentration.
That which is the faculty of wisdom is the power of wisdom; that which is the power of wisdom is the faculty of wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, it is by having developed and cultivated these five faculties that a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints,

Jarāvagga Pubbakoṭṭhakasutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, this body has form, is composed of the four great elements, arises from mother and father, is built up out of boiled rice and porridge, is subject to impermanence, to being worn and rubbed away, to dissolution and disintegration; and consciousness is dependent on it. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how is it, venerable sir, that the body is impermanent? “Ānanda, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Thus, Ānanda, the body is impermanent. “But, venerable sir, how is it that the body is subject to being worn and rubbed away? “Ānanda, the body is worn away by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the touch of flies and mosquitoes, wind and sun and creeping things; it is worn away by ill-spoken, unwelcome, and disagreeable sounds and words. Thus, Ānanda, the body is subject to being worn and rubbed away. “But, venerable sir, how is it that the body is subject to dissolution and disintegration? “Ānanda, when this body comes to a state of final Nibbāna through the exhaustion of the life-faculty, it lies there unwasted, free from appetites, a mere heap of bones, consciousness having vanished. Thus, Ānanda, the body is subject to dissolution and disintegration. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the body is impermanent? “Because of birth, Ānanda, the body is impermanent. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the body is subject to being worn and rubbed away? “Because of aging, Ānanda, the body is subject to being worn and rubbed away. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the body is subject to dissolution and disintegration? “Because of death, Ānanda, the body is subject to dissolution and disintegration. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why birth itself is impermanent? “Because of becoming, Ānanda, birth is impermanent. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why becoming is subject to being worn and rubbed away? “Because of clinging, Ānanda, becoming is subject to being worn and rubbed away. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why clinging is subject to dissolution and disintegration? “Because of craving, Ānanda, clinging is subject to dissolution and disintegration. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why craving itself is impermanent? “Because of feeling, Ānanda, craving is impermanent. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why feeling is subject to being worn and rubbed away? “Because of contact, Ānanda, feeling is subject to being worn and rubbed away. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why contact is subject to dissolution and disintegration? “Because of the sixfold base, Ānanda, contact is subject to dissolution and disintegration. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the sixfold base itself is impermanent? “Because of name-and-form, Ānanda, the sixfold base is impermanent.

“But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why name-and-form is subject to being worn and rubbed away? “Because of consciousness, Ānanda, name-and-form is subject to being worn and rubbed away. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why consciousness is subject to dissolution and disintegration? “Because of kamma-formations, Ānanda, consciousness is subject to dissolution and disintegration. “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why kamma-formations themselves are impermanent? “Because of ignorance, Ānanda, kamma-formations are impermanent. “It is, Ānanda, because of ignorance that kamma-formations come to be; because of kamma-formations, consciousness comes to be; because of consciousness, name-and-form comes to be; because of name-and-form, the sixfold base comes to be; because of the sixfold base, contact comes to be; because of contact, feeling comes to be; because of feeling, craving comes to be; because of craving, clinging comes to be; because of clinging, becoming comes to be; because of becoming, birth comes to be; because of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of kamma-formations; with the cessation of kamma-formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base; with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “You are a clansman, Ānanda, and this Dhamma is profound… It is hard for you to understand it quickly. Live with me, Ānanda, as an attendant bhikkhu. A second time… A third time the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “Come, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “The Dhamma has been well expounded. Live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering. That was how the Venerable Ānanda received the going forth under the Blessed One, and that was his full admission. And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Ānanda, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Ānanda became one of the arahants.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Gatehouse.

when developed and cultivated, has the Deathless as its ground, the Deathless as its destination, the Deathless as its final end’ … [and so on] … ‘the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, has the Deathless as its ground, the Deathless as its destination, the Deathless as its final end’?
“I do not go by faith in the Blessed One in this matter, Bhante.”

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was seated not far from the Blessed One, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. Then the Blessed One, with the mind reading the mind of the Venerable Ānanda, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, this concentration of mind is peaceful, this concentration of mind is sublime; it is attained by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, resulting in letting go. It is this concentration of mind, Ānanda, that you have not yet developed, not cultivated, not made much of, not mastered, and not familiarized yourself with, such that when you were seated not far from me, having folded your legs crosswise, set your body erect, and established mindfulness before you, you did not perceive me or know me. “Indeed, Bhante, this concentration of mind is peaceful, this concentration of mind is sublime; it is attained by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, resulting in letting go. It is this concentration of mind, Bhante, that I have not yet developed, not cultivated, not made much of, not mastered, and not familiarized myself with, such that when I was seated not far from the Blessed One, having folded my legs crosswise, set my body erect, and established mindfulness before me, I did not perceive the Blessed One or know the Blessed One. “Good, good, Ānanda! This concentration of mind is peaceful, this concentration of mind is sublime; it is attained by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, resulting in letting go. It is this concentration of mind, Ānanda, that you have not yet developed, not cultivated, not made much of, not mastered, and not familiarized yourself with, such that when you were seated not far from me, having folded your legs crosswise, set your body erect, and established mindfulness before you, you did not perceive me or know me. Ānanda, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, Ānanda, regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form—these all, on the basis of this very form, cling to it. Whatever ascetics or brahmins, Ānanda, regard feeling as self... regard perception as self... regard volitional formations as self... regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness—these all, on the basis of this very consciousness, cling to it. If, Ānanda, one does not cling to anything in the world, does not take a stand upon anything in the world, then one is called ‘one who does not cling’ (anupādā). For one who does not cling, there is no becoming; for one who has no becoming, there is no birth; for one who is not born, there is no aging and death;

for one who is not subject to aging and death, there is no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair. Thus, there is simply the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. ‘This is the end of suffering,’ Ānanda, is said in reference to this. Ānanda, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. And what, Ānanda, is the origin of these four nutriments? Contact is their origin. And what is the origin of contact? The sixfold sense base is its origin. And what is the origin of the sixfold sense base? Name-and-form is its origin. And what is the origin of name-and-form? Consciousness is its origin. And what is the origin of consciousness? Volitional formations are its origin. And what is the origin of volitional formations? Ignorance is their origin. Thus, Ānanda, from ignorance as a requisite condition come volitional formations; from volitional formations as a requisite condition comes consciousness; from consciousness as a requisite condition comes name-and-form; from name-and-form as a requisite condition comes the sixfold sense base; from the sixfold sense base as a requisite condition comes contact; from contact as a requisite condition comes feeling; from feeling as a requisite condition comes craving; from craving as a requisite condition comes clinging; from clinging as a requisite condition comes becoming; from becoming as a requisite condition comes birth; from birth as a requisite condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the sixfold sense base; from the cessation of the sixfold sense base comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; from the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. ‘This is the end of suffering,’ Ānanda, is said in reference to this.”

Venerable sir, for a noble disciple who has faith, who has aroused energy, whose mindfulness is established, and whose mind is concentrated, it is to be expected that he will understand thus:"

6. Sūkarakhatavagga Sālasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Sālā, a brahmin village.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, just as whatever animals there are that belong to the animal realm, the lion, the king of beasts, is declared to be their chief—in terms of strength, speed, and courage;”
In the same way, monks, whatever states are conducive to enlightenment, the faculty of wisdom is declared to be their foremost, that is, for the sake of enlightenment.
And what, monks, are the states conducive to enlightenment?
The faculty of faith, monks, is a state conducive to enlightenment; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of energy is a factor conducive to enlightenment; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of mindfulness is a factor conducive to enlightenment; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of concentration is a factor conducive to enlightenment; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of wisdom is a state conducive to enlightenment; it leads to enlightenment.

Just as, monks, whatever creatures there are among the animals, the lion, the king of beasts, is declared to be their chief—in terms of strength, speed, and courage—even so, monks, whatever states are conducive to enlightenment, the faculty of wisdom is declared to be their chief, namely, for the sake of enlightenment.
First.

Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Mallas at a town of the Mallas named Uruvelakappa.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

Of which four?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of concentration.

For the wise noble disciple, bhikkhus, faith is established in accordance with that [wisdom]; energy is established in accordance with that; mindfulness is established in accordance with that; and concentration is established in accordance with that. Thus ends the second [sutta].

The one practicing for realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the one practicing for realization of the fruit of once-returning; the one practicing for realization of the fruit of non-returning; the one practicing for realization of the fruit of arahantship; and the one who has entered the fixed course of rightness. These, bhikkhus, are the five trainees.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

“Is there, monks, a method by means of which a monk who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, might know: ‘I am a trainee’; and a monk who is one beyond training, standing on the plane of one beyond training, might know:
‘I am one beyond training’? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One...

“There is, monks, a method by means of which a monk who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, might know: ‘I am a trainee’; and a monk who is one beyond training, standing on the plane of one beyond training, might know: ‘I am one beyond training.’”
And what, bhikkhus, is that method by means of which a bhikkhu who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, understands:
‘I am a trainee’? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is a trainee understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’
‘the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this too, monks, is a method by means of which a bhikkhu who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, understands: ‘I am a trainee.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu who is a trainee reflects thus:
‘Is there indeed anyone else outside this [teaching], whether a recluse or a brahmin, who teaches such a true, real, and factual Dhamma as the Blessed One does?
He understands thus:
‘There is indeed no one else outside this [teaching], whether a recluse or a brahmin, who teaches such a true, real, and factual Dhamma as the Blessed One does.’
This, monks, is another method by means of which a monk who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, understands: "I am a trainee.
Furthermore, monks, a monk who is a trainee understands the five faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

"Whatever their destination, whatever their supreme goal, whatever their fruit, and whatever their consummation may be—he does not dwell having touched these with the body, but rather sees them by piercing through them with wisdom.
This, monks, is another method by means of which a monk who is a trainee, standing on the plane of a trainee, understands: 'I am a trainee.'"
And what, bhikkhus, is the method by means of which a bhikkhu who is beyond training, standing on the plane of one beyond training, understands: ‘I am one beyond training’?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is beyond training understands the five faculties:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

"Whatever their destination, whatever their supreme goal, whatever their fruit, and whatever their consummation may be—he dwells having touched these with his body, and he sees them by piercing through them with wisdom.
This, monks, is the method by means of which a bhikkhu who is beyond training, standing on the plane of one beyond training, understands: 'I am one beyond training.'"
Furthermore, monks, a monk who is beyond training understands the six faculties:

"The eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, and the mind-faculty—these six faculties will cease entirely, in every way, completely, and without remainder; and other six faculties will not arise anywhere or in anything. Thus he understands.
“This too, bhikkhus, is a method by means of which a bhikkhu who is beyond training, standing on the plane of one beyond training, understands: ‘I am one beyond training.
This was the third.

6. The Chapter on the Wild Boar’s Footprint:

The Discourse on Footprints “Bhikkhus, just as whatever footprints of forest animals there may be, they are all encompassed within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is declared to be their foremost because of its great size;”
"In the same way, monks, whatever states lead to enlightenment, the faculty of wisdom is declared to be the foremost among them, that is, for the sake of enlightenment.
And what, monks, are the states that lead to enlightenment?
The faculty of faith, monks, is a state that leads to enlightenment."
The faculty of energy is a foundation; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of mindfulness is a foundation; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of concentration is a foundation; it leads to enlightenment.
The faculty of wisdom is the footprint; it leads to enlightenment.

Just as, monks, whatever footprints of forest animals there may be, they all fit within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them because of its size;
even so, monks, whatever footprints lead to enlightenment, the faculty of wisdom is declared the foremost among them because of its leading to enlightenment.
The Fourth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 48.56 The Book of the Sixes (Chaḷaṅgavagga) Chapter 6: The Chapter on the Boar’s Cave (Sūkarakhatavagga) Discourse on Being Established (Paṭiṭṭhitasaṁyutta) “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is established in five things and possesses four things, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life. “And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu established in five things? Here, a bhikkhu is established in virtue; he is established in concentration; he is established in wisdom; he is established in liberation; and he is established in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is established in these five things. “And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu possess four things? Here, a bhikkhu possesses the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; he possesses the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training; he possesses the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training; and he possesses the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses these four things. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is established in these five things and possesses these four things, he is capable of attaining the destruction of the taints in this very life.”
“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu established in one thing, the five faculties become developed, well-developed.
What is that one thing?
Diligence.”
"And what, monks, is diligence?
Here, monks, a monk guards the mind against the taints and against phenomena associated with the taints.

The faculty of energy also reaches the fulfillment of its development.
The faculty of mindfulness also reaches the fulfillment of its development.
The faculty of concentration also reaches the fulfillment of its development.
The faculty of wisdom also reaches fulfillment through development.
"In this way too, monks, for a monk established in even a single dharma, the five faculties become developed, well-developed.

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having just attained full enlightenment.

The faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, tends toward the Deathless, and culminates in the Deathless. The faculty of energy … [and so on] … [The faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunge into the Deathless, tend toward the Deathless, and culminate in the Deathless.]
The faculty of mindfulness …pe… the faculty of concentration …pe… the faculty of wisdom,
when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its final goal, and culminates in the Deathless.
"These five faculties, when developed and cultivated, have the deathless as their ground, the deathless as their destination,
and the deathless as their consummation. Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One's mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm— likewise [vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One].

Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:

The five faculties, when developed and cultivated, have the Deathless as their ground, the Deathless as their destination, and the Deathless as their consummation.

The faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, has the Deathless as its ground, the Deathless as its destination, and the Deathless as its consummation. …pe… The faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, has the Deathless as its ground, the Deathless as its destination, and the Deathless as its consummation.

The Chapter on the Boar’s Cave (Sūkarakhatavagga)
The Discourse on the Boar’s Cave.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the Boar’s Cave.
There the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, seeing what benefit does a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed act with the highest degree of devotion toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching?

“Venerable sir, it is because he sees the unsurpassed security from bondage that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed acts with the highest degree of devotion toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
“Sāriputta, seeing the unsurpassed security from bondage, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed acts with the highest devotion toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching.
And what, Sāriputta, is that unsurpassed security from bondage, seeing which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed acts with the highest devotion toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching?
“Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed develops the faculty of faith, which leads to peace and leads to enlightenment;”
He develops the faculty of energy …pe… he develops the faculty of mindfulness … he develops the faculty of concentration …
“He develops the faculty of wisdom that leads to peace and leads to enlightenment.

This, venerable sir, is the unsurpassed security from bondage, considering which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed conducts himself with the highest devotion toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”

"For this, Sāriputta, is the unsurpassed security from bondage, seeing which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed conducts himself with the highest reverence toward the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata’s teaching.
